﻿TECH — UNIT 5 · PART 1 MASTER OUTLINE
Game Design Studio — Explore Gaming
CURRENT CAPTAIN GO 2026-11-12: Unit 5 Part 1 has SEVEN consecutive days. Day1–4 original LEARN guides remain unchanged. NEW Day5 3050105 PERFORM: TurboWarp DESKTOP fundamentals skill lab. NEW Day6 3050106 ASSESSMENT: four short Major sections plus half-day previously graded recovery. NEW Day7 3050107 FINAL PERFORM: adapt old Day5 click-to-score prototype into functioning milestone; use posted Major feedback to recover weak answers. The historical old Day5 source retained below is ARCHIVAL only; never reuse its 305010530049 Q30049 full key in a changed assignment. Actual Collector scan found zero matching old Day5 responses but the legacy Question Bank record remains frozen. Current source overrides stale five-day statements below. No standalone Recovery mode, student release or Show changes. TurboWarp desktop installed in lab; turbowarp.org and scratch.mit.edu blocked.


PART 1 REPAIRED DAY SPECIFICATIONS — SOURCE OF TRUTH (2026-11-12)
DAY5 | 3050105 | PERFORM | TurboWarp Desktop Fundamentals
Target: Navigate the installed editor, create and distinguish sprites and backdrops, use Costumes/Code/Sounds, create a score variable, launch/stop scripts, save/reopen a .sb3 and explain a repeatable test. Students build a temporary practice sandbox, NOT the Part milestone. Never open a blocked web URL. 50 min: 5 warm-up/launch; 7 editor tour; 8 add library sprite and draw second custom sprite; 6 change costume and Stage backdrop; 7 make score variable and green-flag event set score to 0 then change by 1; 5 save/reopen .sb3 and restart test; 7 Daily evidence; 5 close/Studio as feasible. Novice steps must name every menu, tab, exact block/category and expected result; include troubleshooting hints.
Daily QID Q30070, full key 305010530070: A new student wants two separately controlled sprites, a score starting at zero, and a way to test their work. Explain where to add/draw sprites, which tool creates the score, and how the green flag and Stop controls support a repeatable test.
Rubric 0–100: 90–100 accurately distinguishes separate sprites, score variable, event controls, and explains a repeatable reset test; 70–89 identifies relevant tools and a valid start/stop/reset check; 50–69 partial understanding or missing a tool/test; below 50 insufficient or incorrect. Scenario independent of own project.
DAY6 | 3050106 | ASSESSMENT | Game Design & TurboWarp Foundations
Target: Demonstrate taught history, player-centered design, fairness, game studio roles, ethical AI and tool fundamentals. Brief non-answer-giving notes; roughly 25 min for 4 short separate Major sections and Form submissions, 25 min recovery of already graded Daily work. No software project in assessment. Major uses exactly 305010639991 through 305010639994, one equal-weight Skyward Major.
SECTION 1 / 305010639991: Compare early Pong-style games with modern games. Name one technology change affecting what designers can build, and a simple UI/control design that helps a younger player, explaining the benefit.
Rubric: 90–100 accurate change, specific feasible UI/control and insightful player-centered reason; 70–89 all three sound; 50–69 partially correct or vague; below 50 insufficient.
SECTION 2 / 305010639992: In a falling-object game hazards spawn directly on the player. Identify the fairness problem, propose one rule change, and explain a repeatable before/after test with an observable outcome.
Rubric: 90–100 precise cause, feasible correction and controlled comparable test; 70–89 valid problem/fix/test; 50–69 incomplete; below 50 insufficient.
SECTION 3 / 305010639993: A game studio wants AI to make all its visuals without reviewing them. Name two studio jobs and how they work together, then give one responsible check before AI-created material is used.
Rubric: 90–100 accurate roles, meaningful collaboration and specific ethical/quality check; 70–89 both roles and sound safeguard; 50–69 weak connection/safeguard; below 50 insufficient.
SECTION 4 / 305010639994: A game needs separate Player and Enemy objects and a score reset to 0 on every restart. Explain which TurboWarp tools/blocks supply sprites, score and start event, and how to test a repeated reset.
Rubric: 90–100 correct sprite/variable/event and repeatable test; 70–89 sound tools and workable reset check; 50–69 partial tool/test reasoning; below 50 insufficient.
DAY7 | 3050107 | FINAL PERFORM | One-Button Arcade Prototype
Use the existing old 3050105 project instructions as editorial basis but remove its question/key and blocked website direction. Students open installed TurboWarp desktop, make score variable, set it to 0 on green flag, add click-to-score behavior capped at 5, show 'You win!' on fifth click, test 0/4/5/6 clicks and restart, save/reopen .sb3 and demonstrate functional milestone. Around 25 min milestone completion/test/show and 20 min recovery of scored Day6 Major sections (only after feedback posted) or previously graded Daily work; 5 min transitions/save. No new ordinary mastery key; project demonstrated by working artifact and teacher observation. If Major feedback delayed, reschedule those corrections instead of pretending they were recovered. No standalone Recovery day.
ARCHIVAL NOTICE: Old DAYID 3050105 source below is historical reference to adapt into Day7 only. Its Q30049 and full key 305010530049 remain immutable in the Collector, never silently reassigned.


FIVE UNIT PILLARS
1. TEKS: §126.18(c)(3)(B–C), (4)(A–C), supporting §126.18(c)(1) prior algorithms and §126.18(c)(2) tool knowledge. Pinned keys 30049–30058 in Personal TEKS Register.
2. Tools: TurboWarp/Scratch-style sprites, events, input, loops, variables, sensing, simple code; paper planning is equivalent conceptual practice but not evidence that software ran.
3. Core principle: Fun is intentionally designed through clear rules, player action, feedback, fair constraints and testing.
4. Industry/careers: game design versus development, arcades and hardware/software evolution, UI/UX, 2D/3D and VR, AI and global market trends, roles in a studio.
5. Deliverable: mini-games → guided Turkey Escape → student-choice playable capstone with final major assessment and showcase.


PART ONE SCOPE
GRADE 7 MASTERY ACCESSIBILITY (CURRENT): Preserve registered question identities, rubrics and evidence criteria while using one or two short typed answers per mastery question (never three). Add brief selected-response checks or accessible activities for additional rigor; keep reading concise. For Day 1 Q30054, Part A is an untyped 3D-design choice; Parts B and C are the only written responses. All five JISD offline lessons must present the same parts as HTML.


Day 1 LEARN: What is game design, the industry now, historical shifts Pong to Fortnite, 3D impact (Q30053 and Q30054).
Day 2 LEARN: game studio careers, UI/UX, audience-specific design and testing (Q30051 and Q30052).
Day 3 LEARN: game loops, fairness, prototyping, testing and design improvements (Q30049 and Q30050).
Day 4 LEARN: global gaming trends, platforms, access, and responsible AI in studio development (Q30055 and Q30056). VR deferred for separate later instruction; keep this lesson centered on global trends and AI.
Day 5 PERFORM: TurboWarp Desktop Fundamentals NEW 3050105, Daily key 305010530070. Day 6 ASSESSMENT NEW 3050106, Major four sections 305010639991–305010639994. Day 7 FINAL PERFORM NEW 3050107, adapted original click-to-score milestone with post-feedback Major recovery. Old Day5 source and 305010530049 archived; no new mastery on Day7.
Fifty-minute lessons include explicit warm-up, delivery, practice, student evidence, closing and transitions. Creative Studio is an optional pathway for additional experiments within one shared response and must not become recovery work. Do not introduce unapproved software/accounts. All student-facing links are to approved TurboWarp URL or teacher-provided materials.


SOURCE REGISTRY AND PINNING
Q30049 | §126.18(c)(3)(B)
QUESTION: A student wants to create a game where a character avoids falling objects. Identify a suitable digital tool, describe the game's essential controls and rules, and explain how you would build and test a simple first version before adding extra features.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Demonstrates a suitable tool choice, practical first prototype, clear rules and a meaningful test. Approaches: Workable but incomplete plan. Did Not Meet: Lacks feasible design or test. Exceeds: Explains how test findings would guide prioritization. Judge holistically, not by per-part points.
Q30050 | §126.18(c)(3)(B)
QUESTION: Playtesters say a game is frustrating because falling objects sometimes appear directly on the player. Explain the design problem, propose two changes, and describe how you would test whether those changes improve the experience.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Identifies an unfair mechanic, offers two relevant changes and a practical comparative test. Approaches: Partial changes or weak testing. Did Not Meet: No credible improvement. Exceeds: Considers tradeoffs between fairness, randomness and challenge. Judge holistically.
Q30051 | §126.18(c)(3)(C)
QUESTION: A game studio is making a new arcade game. Explain the difference between game design and game development. Describe how a game designer, programmer and playtester contribute to creating and improving the finished game.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Distinguishes design from implementation and correctly explains each role's contribution to an iterative process. Approaches: Partially distinguishes roles. Did Not Meet: Conflates responsibilities without demonstrating a design process. Exceeds: Explains how feedback moves between roles. Holistic rubric.
Q30052 | §126.18(c)(3)(C)
QUESTION: Two studios are developing games for different audiences: one for young beginners and another for experienced competitive players. Explain how their teams might use the design process to make different decisions about controls, difficulty, instructions and testing.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Links player needs to concrete design choices and a reasonable testing or revision process in both situations. Approaches: Relevant but underdeveloped comparisons. Did Not Meet: Overlooks audience or the design process. Exceeds: Analyzes a meaningful design tradeoff. Holistic rubric.
Q30053 | §126.18(c)(4)(A)
QUESTION: Compare the early arcade game Pong with the modern game Fortnite. Explain two technological changes and how each changed game design or player experience.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Gives two accurate technological changes and explains meaningful gameplay consequences. Approaches: Identifies changes with weak consequences. Did Not Meet: Unsupported or inaccurate comparisons. Exceeds: Connects technical capabilities to changing design possibilities and constraints. Holistic rubric.
Q30054 | §126.18(c)(4)(A)
QUESTION: Explain how 3D technology changed game design, including one player benefit and one limitation.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Correctly explains a technology-driven design change, a credible player benefit and a relevant limitation. Approaches: Partially accurate or insufficiently explained. Did Not Meet: Assumes advancement guarantees better experience without analysis. Exceeds: Connects player needs or accessibility to the tradeoff. Holistic rubric.
Q30055 | §126.18(c)(4)(B)
QUESTION: Gaming has expanded across consoles, computers, phones and online services. Choose two trends affecting the industry. Explain how each could influence the games developers make and the people who play them.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Identifies two genuine trends and explains plausible effects on development and audiences. Approaches: Identifies trends without adequate connections. Did Not Meet: Unsupported generalizations. Exceeds: Recognizes business, access or ethical tradeoffs. Holistic rubric.
Q30056 | §126.18(c)(4)(B)
QUESTION: A game studio is considering AI tools to help create characters, dialogue or game levels. Explain two possible benefits and two potential problems. Recommend one responsible way the studio could use AI while protecting the player experience.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Gives two defensible benefits, two distinct risks and a justified responsible-use recommendation. Approaches: Relevant considerations with limited reasoning. Did Not Meet: Lacks credible analysis. Exceeds: Includes quality assurance, creator rights, fairness or player trust in the decision. Holistic rubric.
Q30057 | §126.18(c)(4)(C)
QUESTION: A student understands how to move a character using TurboWarp blocks but must now learn an unfamiliar game-building tool. Explain which programming ideas should transfer, what may work differently, and how the student could test a first movement feature.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Transfers relevant programming concepts, identifies plausible tool differences and proposes a practical first test. Approaches: Partial transfer or incomplete test. Did Not Meet: Treats tools as unrelated or lacks viable approach. Exceeds: Explains how comparison and debugging accelerate learning. Holistic rubric.
Q30058 | §126.18(c)(4)(C)
QUESTION: You already know how to make a falling object move repeatedly in a game. Now you want a moving enemy that follows a player instead. Explain which parts of your original algorithm you could reuse, which must change, and how you would check whether the new behavior works.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Meets: Identifies reusable logic, necessary changes and meaningful verification. Approaches: Recognizes some transferable logic but misses an important adaptation or test. Did Not Meet: Cannot connect behaviors. Exceeds: Describes useful edge cases or alternative implementations. Holistic rubric.


AUTHORITATIVE DAY MASTER OUTLINE — FULL CONTENT FOR HTML (NOT DERIVED FROM OFFLINE GUIDE)
DAYID 3050101 | TECH | UNIT 5 | PART 1 | DAY 1 | LEARN Focused
TITLE: How Technology Changed Game Design
STATUS: Captain GO approved Day 1; current Q30053/Q30054 prompts and rubrics were overwritten and verified in the Personal TEKS Register. HTML implementation includes Pong, Fortnite, 3D and Future Sight. VR is deferred.
DAY SUMMARY FOR CAPTAIN
TEKS §126.18(c)(4)(A): Explain how changes in technology throughout history have impacted various areas of study.
Purpose: Introduce the field of game design and explain how historical technological changes transformed its possibilities, from Pong to Fortnite, with a focused explanation of 3D gaming.
Sequence: Pong Warm-Up → (1) What is game design? → (2) The field today: jobs and pathways → (3) How did we get here? Pong, Fortnite, milestones → (4) What changed and why? teacher-led cause-and-effect discussion → independent Q30053 and Q30054 → Future Sight reflection.
Learning Leaders 1–3 teach using specific Pause / Ask / Listen / Ask for Questions / handoff directions. Teacher guides Section 4 using noninteractive questions and collapsed Reveal Facts. Mastery evidence Q30053 and Q30054 both addresses §126.18(c)(4)(A).
LEARNING TARGET — STUDENT DISPLAY
I can explain how changes in technology throughout history changed what game designers can create and how players experience games.
TEACHER-ONLY DESIGN RULES
All facts needed for mastery appear in THIS guide. Outside videos and webpages are optional TEACHER-BOARD ENHANCEMENTS because students' Blocksi restrictions prevent reliable access; never require students to open external sites, watch a video, use another day's guide, or research independently. Aim for 1–2-minute selected excerpts, not full talks. Avoid treating business models, economics, psychology or international popularity as technological innovations by themselves; connect them to enabling devices, networks and software. Independent evidence tests technology → design change → player consequence, not whether new games are more fun.
TIMING — INTERNAL ONLY, DO NOT SHOW IN STUDENT HTML
Warm-Up 5m; sections 1–3 6m+6m+8m; teacher discussion 9m; mastery Q30053/Q30054 12m; Temperature/Creative Studio 2m; transitions 2m = 50m. The Creative Studio and its distinct evidence follow current SOP; keep enrichment concise and protect mastery time.
WARM-UP — CONNECT TO PLAYER EXPERIENCE (5m)
Illustration: original Pong screenshot or clean two-paddle diagram, embedded locally in HTML with alt text and factual source. Explain: In Pong, players move paddles up and down, bounce a square ball across the screen and score when the other paddle misses. Imagine a NEW Pong-inspired game with levels; do not imply original Pong included levels.
Exact prompt: As someone gets better at this new version of Pong, what could you change to keep the game interesting or challenging? Explain why your idea might work.
Student response label: Your answer. OPTIONAL Extra Help collapsed: Think of a game you know well. What makes you want to play again after you understand the basic rules? Do not include answer examples in the prompt. Xtra participation only, existing submission identity.
SECTION 1 — LEARNING LEADER 1: WHAT IS GAME DESIGN? (6m)
Student-facing reading: Game design is the work of planning what players do, the rules they follow, the goals they pursue and the feedback they receive. A game designer decides how a player's choices shape an experience. Unlike simply playing a game, designing one means predicting what other people will understand, try, enjoy or find confusing. Designers use prototypes and playtests to revise their ideas. For example, Pong's designers needed a clear paddle-and-ball rule anyone could learn quickly, while Fortnite's designers must coordinate movement, 3D spaces, matches and updates. Game design matters because it turns technology into understandable, usable experiences. Artists, programmers, sound designers and testers work alongside designers; one person can fill multiple roles in a small studio.
Real-world professional example: Civilization designer Sid Meier has spoken to game developers about 'interesting decisions': a game needs meaningful choices, not just impressive graphics. That is an industry design perspective, not a separate TEKS target.
Learning Leader script EXACT: 'Read the paragraph aloud. PAUSE READING. ASK THE CLASS: What is one decision a game designer makes that a game player does not? LISTEN to two answers. FOLLOW UP: How would a player notice that choice? PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS. Then say: The next leader will show what this field looks like today. PASS TO LEARNING LEADER 2.'
Optional teacher-display source: Sid Meier's Interesting Decisions (GDC professional talk), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WggIdtrqgKg ; source explanation https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/video-sid-meier-explores-interesting-decisions-in-gameplay . Use only a brief teacher-selected excerpt if available; all required concepts are above.
SECTION 2 — LEARNING LEADER 2: WHAT IS GAME DESIGN LIKE TODAY? (6m)
Student-facing reading: Today, game design is a worldwide field. A studio may employ game designers, software developers, 3D artists, sound designers, writers, user-experience designers, producers and playtesters. Designers can learn through school computer science, digital art, mathematics, writing, technical programs, college courses, portfolios and making small playable games; there is no single required pathway. Today's games run on consoles, PCs and smartphones. Teams decide how to use available graphics, memory, controllers, online networking and 3D environments. Fortnite is a useful example: its designers support a 3D playable island, moving cameras, interactive environments and online matches. Some modern games use free-to-play purchases and cosmetic shops; these are business/design choices supported by software and connected distribution, not technologies by themselves. Powerful graphics can expand choices, but cannot guarantee a game is fun or fair.
Worldwide perspectives: Nintendo's handheld and console traditions show that convenience and well-designed controls can matter as much as visual realism; internationally connected games and mobile distribution let studios reach audiences beyond one arcade or one country. Avoid claiming all countries or studios design alike.
Career/education connection for student leader: ASK: Which school subject could help a game designer do their work? Take two answers, then explain that coding, visual art, math, storytelling and collaboration are all useful routes. No specific degree is required for every role; demonstrated work and skills matter.
Learning Leader script EXACT: 'Read aloud. PAUSE READING. ASK THE CLASS: How might designing a game for a phone differ from designing one for a television and controller? LISTEN to two ideas. FOLLOW UP: Which difference is caused by the device itself? PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS. Introduce the next leader: How did games change enough to make all these choices possible? PASS TO LEARNING LEADER 3.'
Optional teacher-display professional source: Scopely systems designer Evan Losi on mobile free-to-play systems, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSyt0alpoyg ; professional context https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/video-system-design-advice-for-mobile-free-to-play-games . For middle school, briefly paraphrase, do not assign lengthy specialist talk.
SECTION 3 — LEARNING LEADER 3: HOW DID WE GET HERE? (8m)
Student-facing reading: How did the field become this way? Atari's 1972 arcade Pong used two paddles, a square ball and simple 2D graphics. Players moved paddles vertically; a miss gave the opponent a point. Limited hardware made simple controls and visual feedback practical. Coin-operated arcade settings favored games easy for strangers to start. Home consoles later moved play to televisions; cartridges allowed a library of different games. Better processors, memory and graphics hardware enabled longer, more complex games with richer sound and scenery. Moving from flat 2D playfields to navigable 3D environments required software that draws objects from changing camera positions and controls that let players move through a world. Network and server technologies then made large online multiplayer matches and repeated content updates practical. Fortnite combines these later capabilities: a detailed 3D island, camera and movement controls, online matches and changing content. Its modern design was not possible on Pong's original circuitry. Phone gaming and touchscreens created different design priorities, including portability and shorter sessions. Poker influenced video game design through bluffing, calculated risks, and making decisions without knowing everything. Game designers use these ideas to create suspense and meaningful player choices. Technology opened new possibilities; designers still decide which to use.
Four historically grounded comparison anchors for teacher board: (1) Pong 1972: 2D paddle input and instant scoring; (2) cartridge home consoles: switch games at home; (3) 3D-capable computers/consoles: render navigable environments and cameras; (4) Fortnite: modern 3D world, online multiplayer and continuing software updates. Do not imply every innovation debuted in the named example.
DIRECT PONG vs FORTNITE EVIDENCE — explicitly teach BEFORE independent Q30053: Pong: simple 2D playfield, paddle movement, two-player ball returns, score on a miss, stand-alone arcade cabinet. Fortnite: 3D space with player-controlled movement/camera, detailed environments, many networked players and changing online content. Technology change A — stronger graphics/processing and more memory enable rendered 3D worlds and more complex visual feedback. Technology change B — internet networking and servers enable real-time online multiplayer and updates. Students should explain effects independently rather than copy teacher-prewritten completed responses. Benefits of 3D: depth/spatial exploration and wider design options; limitations: a moving camera/complex controls can make navigation harder for beginners, and higher rendering needs can limit older devices. This directly prepares Q30054 without teaching VR.
Learning Leader script EXACT: 'Read the history aloud in short chunks and point to the five examples. PAUSE READING after the home-console milestone. ASK THE CLASS: What changed when people could play different games at home instead of visiting an arcade? Hear one response. Continue reading. PAUSE READING after smartphones. ASK THE CLASS: Which new device or connection changed how and where people play? Hear two responses. PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS. PASS TO THE TEACHER for the final discussion.'
Optional authentic historical source and photographs: Computer History Museum games timeline https://www.computerhistory.org/timeline/graphics-games/ ; Pong history https://www.computerhistory.org/timeline/1972/ ; museum artifacts https://computerhistory.org/stories/computers-and-games-love-story/ . Teacher can display a still or a short authorized excerpt; no student access needed.
SECTION 4 — TEACHER: WHAT CHANGED AND WHY? (9m)
Goal: Draw causal connections between technological shifts and design choices, then prepare students to reason independently. No multiple-choice radio buttons, answer selectors or text submission inputs during group discussion. Place each question onscreen; leave facts hidden in expandable REVEAL FACTS panel until student responses have been heard. For each prompt ask for 1–2 ideas, then reveal only as needed. Keep questions accessible, not prescriptive answers.
Discussion 1 prompt: 'Pong used two paddles, one ball and a simple screen. What design choices made sense given the technology and the arcade setting?'
REVEAL FACTS 1: Pong's limited electronics displayed basic 2D shapes and rapid feedback. A few clear controls supported a quick first play; coin-per-play economics added pressure for repeatable rounds. Technology and business influenced designers in different ways. Source: The Strong Museum of Play, https://www.museumofplay.org/games/pong/ .
Discussion 2 prompt: 'What became possible when game systems grew powerful enough to show and move through a 3D world, rather than a flat Pong playfield?'
REVEAL FACTS 2: Faster graphics hardware, processors and memory made real-time 3D scenes and moving camera views practical. Designers could build depth-based exploration and new movement choices, but also had to help players manage the camera and navigation. Epic Games describes Fortnite's 3D rendering and its visual-detail technology: https://www.fortnite.com/news/drop-into-the-next-generation-of-fortnite-battle-royale-powered-by-unreal-engine-5-1 . Do not require pupils to master engine names.
Discussion 3 prompt: 'Why could Fortnite support online matches among many players and change over time, while the original Pong cabinet could not?'
REVEAL FACTS 3: Network connections, servers, contemporary computing and updateable software make real-time online play and new content possible. These capabilities create additional design challenges, including fairness among players, reliability and keeping systems understandable. Improved technology adds capabilities, not automatic enjoyment.
Discussion 4 optional if time: 'What else besides hardware influences game design—such as poker, storytelling or how a game earns money? Which changes rely on new technology?'
REVEAL FACTS 4: Bluffing and incomplete information in poker have influenced how developers think about believable game AI; GDC presenter Dave Mark explicitly drew this connection. Designer Sid Meier discusses players' decisions and psychology. Free-to-play economies and battle passes change incentives and progression; internet distribution, software updates and payment systems help support these designs. These are cross-field influences, but only the technology-to-design link directly satisfies today's TEKS. Teacher sources: https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/video-what-playing-poker-taught-me-about-designing-game-ai ; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MtzCLd93SyU ; https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016423/Free-to-Play-Game-Design .
Teacher closing question: 'Compare Pong and Fortnite: name one historical technological change, what new design possibility it enabled, and how it affected players. Then consider one benefit and one drawback of 3D play.' Release students to respond independently.
INDEPENDENT MASTERY — TWO REGISTERED TARGETS, DISTINCT SUBMISSIONS (12m)
Q30053 | §126.18(c)(4)(A) | existing permanent key and holistic rubric preserved:
CURRENT REGISTERED QUESTION Q30053: Compare the early arcade game Pong with the modern game Fortnite. Identify two different technological changes, explain what each allowed game designers to create, and describe how those changes affected players.
CAPTAIN-APPROVED DAY 1 STUDENT-FACING CONTEXT/WORDING: Compare the early arcade game Pong with the modern game Fortnite. Identify two different technological changes, explain what each allowed game designers to create, and describe how those changes affected players.
STUDENT-FACING MULTIPART Q30053 (LOW LANGUAGE LOAD): Part A — multiple choice: What technology lets Fortnite players join online matches from different places? Part B — multiple choice: What technology made large, playable 3D worlds more practical? Part C — true/false: Pong's original arcade hardware could run a modern Fortnite-style 3D online match. Part D — one short written explanation (2–3 sentences): How did these TWO technologies change what game designers could create and what players could experience? All choices are assembled with the single short answer into one submission. Q30053 evidence-seeking holistic rubric recognizes accurate student ideas even with simple wording, partial credit for genuine partial reasoning, and avoids grading vocabulary or spelling. Keep permanent evidence key and Form route unchanged.
Q30054 | §126.18(c)(4)(A) | existing permanent key and holistic rubric preserved:
CURRENT REGISTERED QUESTION Q30054: Explain how 3D technology changed game design, including one player benefit and one limitation.
CAPTAIN-APPROVED DAY 1 STUDENT-FACING CONTEXT/WORDING (now registered and used in the revised HTML): Explain how 3D technology changed game design, including one player benefit and one limitation. VR is excluded from today's teaching and student-facing question; reserve it for a later full lesson.
Q30054 MULTIPART EVIDENCE: Students identify a 3D-enabled design possibility, explain a benefit for players, and explain one limitation. Keep it independent; no VR-specific knowledge. The registered holistic rubric is evidence-seeking: accept accurate student ideas in simple language; recognize partial understanding; reward thoughtful tradeoffs involving navigation, controls, accessibility, hardware, and player experience rather than looking for prescribed vocabulary.
STUDENT-READABLE RECOVERY: All explanatory facts and examples are present in sections 1–4; students who missed discussion can re-read them and open Reveal Facts. No new external resources required. Extra Help may prompt reasoning but never fill their mastery answer.
FUTURE SIGHT — SPECULATIVE INDEPENDENT REFLECTION (XTRA, NOT NEW TEKS MASTERY)
Prompt: 'Future Sight! Imagine a new set of glasses that detects brainwaves and lets someone sit and play games using only their mind. What challenges would a game designer face while planning a game for this new technology? Explain your ideas.' This is a fictional design scenario, not a claim of an existing reliable product. Students transfer design reasoning; do not grade speculative technology as the historical TEKS.
TEKS TEMPERATURE + CREATIVE STUDIO
Display full student-friendly priority TEKS and I-can statement with thumbs confidence and meaningful reflection per CURRENT SOP. Preserve distinct Temperature and Studio participation identities. Creative Studio is a separate short extension with three on-topic ideas, and Future Sight is the primary reflection prompt; do not impose two lengthy independent reflection submissions. Possible studio ideas: museum-caption design comparison, adapting Pong to a smartphone, or short exchange between game designers from different periods.
REGISTRY ALIGNMENT: Captain authorized overwriting unused Q30053/Q30054 prompts and rubrics; registered wording verified before HTML build. No Unit 5 guides have been taught as of 2026-11-09. Maintain source-to-question parity; avoid retroactively changing taught evidence. All student-facing media is optional teacher-display content.
END-OF-DAY QA / BUILD HANDOFF
LEARN mode and priority TEKS visible; three student leaders with Pause/Ask/Listen/Ask for Questions and handoff; teacher Reveal Facts; authentic Pong and Fortnite read-before-test examples; industry roles and education pathways; 3D discussed deeply with benefit/limitation; NO VR on Day 1; teacher media optional; no group input controls; Q30053/Q30054 distinct mastery targets; hypothetical Future Sight reflection; no Venn/debate/Perform; teacher-only pacing, no student dependencies; registry identities and existing HTML/offline/Forms/Show unchanged; pending permanent question version reconciliation before HTML.
INSTRUCTIONAL PATTERN FOR OTHER LEARN DAYS — PROPOSED, NOT AUTHORIZED EDITS
Check every subsequent Day summary in TEKS-first order: state literal priority TEKS, one-sentence target, brief section arc, examples/voices, authentic discussion, and exact pinned mastery evidence. A Learn day should deliver meaningful knowledge before independent evidence; don't add disconnected Practice/Perform tasks. Rotate professional, historical, international, ethical and future perspectives where TEKS relevant; make external media teacher-display optional and text self-sufficient. Apply actual student-leader scripts rather than reading blocks; group discussion display-only. Do not modify other days under this Day 1-only GO.


AUTHORITATIVE COMPLETE MASTER OUTLINE — TECH UNIT 5 PART 1 DAY 2
DAYID 3050102 | LEARN Focused | Inside a Game Studio
TEKS: §126.18(c)(3)(C) — identify how the design process is used in various industries.
LEARNING TARGET: I can explain how game studio specialists cooperate and design for different audiences because each role contributes to planning, building and improving games.
WARM-UP: A new player cannot find the Start button in a beautiful game menu. What might the game team need to change to help that player? Explain your idea.
LEARN: Three student Learning Leaders with read, explicit PAUSE, ASK THE CLASS, listen, follow-up, ask for questions and handoff. No separate Perform activity.
LEARNING LEADER 1 — Who Makes Games?
READ: Professional studios bring together game designers, software programmers, visual artists, audio specialists and playtesters. A designer plans the game's rules, goals and player experience. Developers implement a functioning product: code, assets and interactions. A programmer turns rules into working instructions. A playtester tries an unfinished version, reports confusion or glitches, and provides evidence for revisions. In small indie studios people often perform several roles; large companies may divide responsibilities among departments. Real game careers can grow from coding, art, math, writing and making small portfolio projects.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: What is the difference between planning a game's experience and making that game run?
FOLLOW UP: How could a playtester help both the designer and programmer?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
LEARNING LEADER 2 — UI, UX and Player Trust
READ: User interface (UI) means the controls and information you can see or use: Start, Pause, score, labels and icons. User experience (UX) is how it feels and functions to play: can you find the goal, understand controls, receive feedback and recover from mistakes? Imagine a start screen with a giant decorative title but a tiny, pale Play label; its artwork may be beautiful while newcomers cannot start. A tester observes where someone hesitates; a designer redesigns the menu; a programmer makes the button respond. The team then tests again. Real studio development is a cycle, not one person's perfect first attempt.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: Which part is UI, and which part is UX, when a player cannot find Start?
FOLLOW UP: What observation would prove the redesign helped?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
LEARNING LEADER 3 — Different Audiences Need Different Designs
READ: A young beginner may benefit from large controls, a slower pace, readable hints and clear feedback. Experienced competitive players may welcome optional advanced controls, faster challenges and more strategic decisions. Neither audience is 'better'; a studio designs for the people expected to play. Designers use a process: define who is playing, plan controls and rules, build a small version, watch representative people play, and revise. Industry teams can include accessibility specialists who review color, reading and motor needs. Designing for players' real abilities is both ethical and practical.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: Why should a designer test a beginner's game with actual beginners?
FOLLOW UP: What might competitive players need that beginners do not?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
TEACHER-LED DISCUSSION — group discussion only; no answer controls. For each question, hear class ideas and optionally reveal facts.
DISCUSSION 1: If a Start button looks clear but does nothing, which studio role should help first, and how do the others contribute?
REVEAL FACTS 1: A programmer checks the click event; a designer checks whether the control fits the intended experience; a playtester verifies the repair with a real user. The team communicates findings.
DISCUSSION 2: How might a studio make a game welcoming to a younger beginner without making it boring for an expert?
REVEAL FACTS 2: Different audiences may need adjustable controls, instruction, practice and difficulty. The correct decision comes from observing and testing with each audience; 'make it fun' is too vague.
DISCUSSION 3: Could a small independent game studio operate differently from a huge international studio?
REVEAL FACTS 3: A small team often combines roles; a big team has specialists and handoffs. Both use planning, building, testing and revision. Teacher-board example: https://www.youtube.com/@Gdconf .

DAYID 3050103 | LEARN Focused | Rules, Fairness and Playtesting
TEKS: §126.18(c)(3)(B) — discuss and implement a design process that includes planning and selecting digital tools to develop and refine a prototype or model through trial and error.
LEARNING TARGET: I can plan and test a fair game prototype because design improvements come from observing what players actually experience.
WARM-UP: In a falling-objects game, a rock suddenly appears on top of your character and you lose before you can move. Would you call that challenging or unfair? Explain why.
LEARN: Three student Learning Leaders with read, explicit PAUSE, ASK THE CLASS, listen, follow-up, ask for questions and handoff. No separate Perform activity.
LEARNING LEADER 1 — Design a Core Game Loop
READ: A game loop is a repeatable cycle: a player acts, the system responds, the player receives feedback and decides what to do next. In a falling-object game, the player moves left or right, watches hazards fall, avoids them and earns points. Rules decide what counts as success. Constraints such as time, lives or movement limits give players meaningful decisions. Good feedback includes a score, a visible hit or a sound. A first prototype needs only the essential loop before decorations and extra levels. Designers can plan on paper, then use an approved tool such as TurboWarp to create a small testable version.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: What must a player be able to do before this can count as a working game?
FOLLOW UP: What feedback should happen after success or failure?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
LEARNING LEADER 2 — Challenge Is Not the Same as Unfairness
READ: Difficulty matters, but losing should usually follow a rule a player can understand and have a chance to respond to. If a falling rock spawns exactly where a player stands with no warning, the player may be unable to avoid it. Randomness makes a game less predictable, but it cannot replace clear controls and fair consequences. A warning, safe spawn zone or brief start delay might help. Another game with no challenge at all may become repetitive. Designers examine the audience: younger beginners and competitive experts might need different speed, instructions and feedback. A difficulty curve describes how challenge changes as players gain skills.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: How is a surprising obstacle different from an unavoidable one?
FOLLOW UP: What could a designer observe to tell whether the challenge is fair?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
LEARNING LEADER 3 — Plan, Build, Test, Revise
READ: Game designers use prototypes—small models that test one idea before the entire game is built. A useful first prototype of a falling-object game needs a playable sprite, movement, a falling hazard, a rule for being hit and feedback. The team tests the basic interaction first. During playtesting, one person observes what players actually do, including missed instructions or impossible hazards. Developers record a specific problem, revise one feature and retest with similar players. A comparison between the first and second test offers evidence of improvement. Trial and error is systematic when designers change something for a reason and check the results.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: Why test a simple first version before adding a shop, music and several levels?
FOLLOW UP: How could you prove a change reduced unfair losses?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
TEACHER-LED DISCUSSION — group discussion only; no answer controls. For each question, hear class ideas and optionally reveal facts.
DISCUSSION 1: A prototype has beautiful graphics, but the player cannot move. Is it ready for playtesting?
REVEAL FACTS 1: The essential game loop must function first. The team should prioritize controls and observable results before decorative polish.
DISCUSSION 2: Players report that rocks sometimes appear directly on their heads. What two changes could make this fairer?
REVEAL FACTS 2: Designers could consider safe spawning, warnings or a short response window. The critical requirement is a test that checks whether players now have a reasonable chance to react.
DISCUSSION 3: Why might two students disagree about whether a game is too hard?
REVEAL FACTS 3: Experience and accessibility needs vary. Testing with the intended audience provides better evidence than asking only the developer.

DAYID 3050104 | LEARN Focused | Worldwide Games and Responsible AI
TEKS: §126.18(c)(4)(B) — explain how global trends impact the development of technology.
LEARNING TARGET: I can explain how global gaming trends and AI tools influence game development because studios respond to changing audiences, platforms and responsibilities.
WARM-UP: Imagine your favorite game suddenly becomes playable on a phone in many countries. What might its designers have to change? Explain one possibility.
LEARN: Three student Learning Leaders with read, explicit PAUSE, ASK THE CLASS, listen, follow-up, ask for questions and handoff. No separate Perform activity.
LEARNING LEADER 1 — Games Cross Borders
READ: The games industry is international. Studios in Japan, the United States, South Korea, Finland and many other places create games for local and worldwide audiences. New devices, online connections, translations and digital storefronts help games travel. The rise of phones as gaming devices changed who can play and when. Designers may adapt controls, screen layout, instructions, language, download size and network needs. A game popular on one platform may not transfer unchanged to another. Global trends influence the technology companies build and the products they support.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: What must a studio consider before releasing a game to players using phones in different countries?
FOLLOW UP: Which of those concerns would influence a technology choice?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
LEARNING LEADER 2 — New Ways to Deliver and Pay for Games
READ: Older games were often purchased as cartridges or paid arcade sessions. Today games can be bought as downloads, played online, updated after release or offered free with optional purchases. These business models influence designers' decisions about progress, rewards and ongoing content. Digital distribution, secure payments, online servers and update systems make some models practical, but a shop or battle pass is a business feature, not a technological advancement by itself. Studios should be careful not to confuse pressure to spend with a genuinely good player experience. Player trust, fairness and access matter.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: How might downloadable updates change the work of a studio compared with selling a finished cartridge?
FOLLOW UP: What could go wrong if a studio prioritizes selling upgrades over player trust?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
LEARNING LEADER 3 — AI as a Studio Tool
READ: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools may suggest dialogue, draft character concepts, propose maze layouts and help identify bugs. A human team could review ten draft mazes faster than designing every first idea from scratch, but some generated layouts might be unsolvable, confusing or unfair. Generated art could also raise questions about permission and creators' rights. Responsible studios check outputs for quality, privacy, bias and accessibility; human designers make the final decisions and playtest results. AI is not proof that a game becomes more enjoyable or original. This is a worldwide industry discussion because AI affects creators and audiences differently.
PAUSE AND ASK THE CLASS: Why must humans test an AI-generated maze before using it in a published game?
FOLLOW UP: What is one benefit and one genuine problem a studio should weigh?
PAUSE AND ASK FOR QUESTIONS; hand off to the next leader or teacher.
TEACHER-LED DISCUSSION — group discussion only; no answer controls. For each question, hear class ideas and optionally reveal facts.
DISCUSSION 1: What are TWO genuine global trends affecting games, and how might each change what developers build?
REVEAL FACTS 1: Examples include mobile access, international online audiences, digital updates and AI-supported production. Each trend should be connected to technology and player or developer consequences.
DISCUSSION 2: If a global studio releases a game on phones, what must it change beyond translating the words?
REVEAL FACTS 2: Touchscreen controls, display size, connection limits, device speed and accessible instructions affect the design. Player needs vary.
DISCUSSION 3: Should studios let AI create game levels without checking them? Why not?
REVEAL FACTS 3: Human reviewers must check whether levels are solvable, understandable, fair and respectful of creators' rights. AI's speed is a possible benefit, not a replacement for accountability.

TITLE: One-Button Arcade Challenge
PILLARS: Gaming industry, game-design principles, TurboWarp implementation, fun and fairness, choice-based capstone.
IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: HTML must use the unmodified canonical master shell; questions in the student HTML must elicit every source rubric criterion; on-paper guide is derived AFTER the verified HTML, never the reverse.


LEARNING TARGET
I can turn simple game-design decisions into a playable TurboWarp prototype because clear instructions and feedback connect planning to development.
PRIORITY TEKS
§126.18(c)(3)(B)
TODAY'S MISSION
Build and test a very small click-to-score game, then record one design improvement for its player.
WARM-UP
A player only sees a character and a blank background. What is the first on-screen clue you would add so they know what to do?
RECALL — USE WHAT YOU ALREADY KNOW (NO NEW LESSON)
A sprite is an on-screen game object. Events respond to the green flag or a click. A variable stores the score. A condition checks whether a click should add a point. Review the supplied 'Click the Star Five Times' example only if you need a reminder.
PERFORM — FOLLOW EVERY STEP
1. Open https://turbowarp.org/ on the class-approved device. If a browser warns about leaving the guide, open it in a new tab. You should see a stage on the right, block categories on the left, and a coding area in the middle.
2. In the lower-right Sprite pane, click the existing cat sprite once to select it. You may keep the cat; no artwork is required. Look above the blocks and check that Code is selected.
3. Click the orange Variables category. Choose 'Make a Variable', type score (lowercase), confirm 'For all sprites', and select OK. Check that the score monitor appears on the stage.
4. In the yellow Events category, drag 'when green flag clicked' into the coding area. From Variables attach 'set score to 0' underneath it. From Looks attach 'say [Click me five times!] for [2] seconds'. Click the green flag. Score should show 0 and the sprite should explain the goal.
5. From Events drag 'when this sprite clicked' into an empty part of the coding area. From Control attach 'if < > then'. From Operators insert a green less-than comparison into the diamond. Put the orange score variable in the left side and type 5 on the right side.
6. Inside that IF, attach Variables → 'change score by 1'. Still inside the first IF, place another Control → 'if < > then'. Use Operators → greater-than, place score on the left and 4 on the right; inside it attach Looks → 'say [You win!]'. The second condition belongs inside the first condition.
7. Test in order: green flag → score 0; four clicks → scores 1–4 without victory; fifth click → score 5 with 'You win!'; sixth click → score remains 5; green flag → score resets to 0. If a click does nothing, select the sprite and check the click script is connected. If score grows forever, check that score < 5 encloses 'change score by 1'.
8. Use File → Save to your computer if allowed, or the teacher-approved saving procedure. Keep the saved filename recognizable. If saving is blocked, do not claim it saved; record that for your teacher.
9. Ask a partner to play once. Record ONE observed confusion and ONE specific improvement to try next time. Your teacher checks the actual running project; writing a description alone does not demonstrate functional code.
TIME: 5 warm-up, 4 recall, 4 example/demo, 29 guided build/testing, 5 reflection/Creative Studio, 3 transitions.
SUCCESS CRITERIA
Check that the user can complete the goal and understand the feedback.
EXTRA HELP
Blocks to find: Events (when green flag clicked; when this sprite clicked), Variables (make variable; set score to 0; change score by 1), Control (if then), Operators (<, > and = use comparison blocks; to test at least five, compare score > 4), Looks (say). Build and test ONE event script at a time. If clicking does nothing, confirm the blocks are attached to the sprite, not the Stage. If it wins immediately, reset score and inspect the comparison. If the score keeps growing, add a condition that only allows clicks before winning.
CREATIVE STUDIO
1. Add two costumes for clear click feedback.
2. Make the target move to a new safe position after each click.
3. Change the target score to 3 or 8 and explain how that changes difficulty.
RESOURCES
TurboWarp editor https://turbowarp.org/ ; on-paper block plan printed above for offline completion. No extensions, downloads or account creation required.
50-MINUTE PLAN
5 warm-up; 4 recall; 4 model; 20 guided building/testing; 9 registered mastery Q30049; 5 Creative Studio/reflection; 3 transitions = 50 minutes.
